title: Why Low-Carb Sends Some People's Cholesterol Soaring
hook: The same low-carb diet can leave one person's LDL untouched and send another's climbing — and genetic predisposition to high cholesterol, plus saturated fat intake, tracks the difference.
key_points: Low-carb diets raised LDL cholesterol far more in people genetically predisposed to high cholesterol.
The effect was strongest when the diet was also high in saturated fat.
Genetically unpredisposed people saw much smaller LDL changes on similar diets.
It helps explain why identical-looking diets produce wildly different blood results.
Low-carb is not automatically LDL-raising, nor automatically safe.
The practical move is to re-check your lipid panel after a major diet change.
content_html: Nutrition arguments usually get stuck on whether a diet is good or bad, when the more useful question is for whom. This work makes that concrete: a low-carb diet raised LDL cholesterol much more sharply in people carrying a genetic predisposition to high cholesterol, particularly when what replaced the carbohydrates was heavy in saturated fat. People without that predisposition saw far smaller shifts on similar diets.
extra_html:
That's a satisfying answer to something anyone who's watched friends try the same diet has noticed: one person's numbers barely move, another's LDL jumps enough to alarm their doctor. Both followed the same plan. The difference wasn't discipline — it was how their bodies handle the fat that comes with the plan.

The takeaway isn't "avoid low-carb" or "low-carb is fine." It's that you can't infer your own response from anyone else's, including your own from a decade ago. If you make a substantial change to how you eat, get a lipid panel a few months in — ideally including apoB — and treat those numbers, not the diet's reputation, as the verdict.

related.title: Understanding Cholesterol
related.hook: Cholesterol has a good side and a bad side. Too much of the bad kind builds up in your arteries for years — silently — until it triggers a heart attack or stroke.

related.title: Millions May Be Getting the Wrong Cholesterol Test
related.hook: A new study finds that apoB — a blood test measuring harmful cholesterol particles directly — beats standard LDL testing at identifying who actually needs more intensive treatment.

related.title: Good Fats, Bad Fats
related.hook: Fat isn't the enemy — the type is what matters. Swapping saturated and trans fats for unsaturated ones beats just trying to eat less fat overall.

related.title: The Inherited Heart Risk a Standard Cholesterol Test Misses
related.hook: About 1 in 5 people carry high Lp(a) — an inherited cholesterol particle tied to stroke and cardiac death that routine lipid panels don't measure. One blood test finds it.

flashcards.prompt: Who saw the biggest LDL rise on a low-carb diet?
flashcards.back_html: People genetically predisposed to high cholesterol — especially when the diet was also high in saturated fat. Others saw much smaller changes on similar diets.

flashcards.prompt: What does this finding best explain?

choices.text: Why two people on seemingly identical diets get very different cholesterol results
Why low-carb diets are unsafe for everyone
Why saturated fat has no effect on cholesterol

flashcards.explanation_html: The result is about variation in response, not a blanket verdict. Genetic background plus saturated fat intake predicts who is in the high-response group.

flashcards.prompt: What's the practical takeaway if you're trying a low-carb diet?
flashcards.back_html: Don't assume your response matches anyone else's — get a lipid panel a few months after a major diet change and let your own numbers decide.
